I believe potential jurors usually get a question along the lines of "Do you know of any reason why you couldn't reach a guilty/not-guilty verdict?" which would preclude jury nullification.

What do you mean by that would preclude jury nullification?

it won't work

The juror system is rigged by having the prosecutor disqualify a potential juror for having bias or having intentions of ruining a verdict with jury nullification. The court system in general is rigged with gag orders and blocking evidence for going against the verdict the judge wants.
To be fair, defense attorneys get to disqualify jurors too.

It only takes one to get through the filtering and nullify the BS. As it happens more I guarantee it will be near impossible to stop them, that is if the media gives it publicity. So no, it will never happen.

Along these lines, I could not believe how much the prosecuting attorney kept repeating that our job as jurors was not to determine if the person had done something wrong, only if they had violated the law. Motherfucker, that's NOT how this works. The ENTIRE GODDAMN REASON FOR A JURY TRIAL is so that the commoners can judge the law itself.

This option should be tossed out altogether. The author writes A jury that considers drug laws to be outrageous can nullify. A jury that is aware of the mass inequality in incarceration rates and believes a defendant was targeted via racial profiling can nullify. A jury that believes a harmless defendant is a victim of the prison industrial complex rather than a perpetrator can nullify.

The law should be based on facts not on beliefs or feelings. If you disagree with the law - there is a process in place to change it. The logic applied by the author is the same logic used by vigilantes and is just as wrong.

It's a difficult decision to make, simply because it can be used to justify acts such as lynchings, as is reported in the case referenced (U.S. v. Thomas, 116 F.3d 606 (2d Cir. 1997)), but at the same time, it is also a means of rejected antiquated and unjust laws that would otherwise land a socially innocent person in prison for life, such as in the case of the Occupy Wall Street protester referenced in the article.

In the reference that the article links to (Cornell Law) it says:

Jury nullification is a discretionary act, and is not a legally sanctioned function of the jury. It is considered to be inconsistent with the jury's duty to return a verdict based solely on the law and the facts of the case. The jury does not have a right to nulification...

I think one thing that is important to note is that the legal case referenced in the above link DOES NOT explicitly outline the condoning of jury nullification by the court, as it is technically still against the oath that a juror takes when they promise to uphold the law as it is presented to them. According to the case in question (U.S. v. Thomas, 116 F.3d 606 (2d Cir. 1997)), should the presiding judge find explicit evidence of a jurors intent to reach a engage in nullification, they are to engage in measures to reprimand or dismiss the juror in question, as is evident by claims such as:

"Although nullification may sometimes succeed--because, among other things, it does not come to the attention of a presiding judge before the completion of a jury's work, and jurors are not answerable for nullification after the verdict has been reached--it would be a dereliction of duty for a judge to remain indifferent to reports that a juror is intent on violating his oath."

However, it is also important to note here that nullification is still possible, by means of maintaining secrecy of the intent to nullify, despite being against the oath of the jurors in the first place, AND that the jury has no obligation to answer for their nullifying verdict once it ha been reached. So the loophole isn't so much like, "jurors are permitted to do this," but is rather more like, "jurors can get away with doing this". I just felt that was an important distinction to make.

When we think of "jury nullification," we think of nice happy things like getting a teenager off of a pot conviction or keeping someone who defended himself from police brutality from getting convicted.

But lets think for a second what jury nullification could also be used for. It could be used in a case of a pro-lifer who killed an abortion doctor. It could be used in the case of a police officer who murdered someone on the job. It could be used when a beloved religious figure molests someone.

Jury nullification is a tool that can be used to back a jury member's individual agenda, whether good or bad. Just keep that in mind.
